steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing a new method for open-set semi-supervised object detection, where the unlabeled data contains out-of-distribution objects. Motivate the problem, discuss the limits of the existing approach, and summarize our method and contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- SSL and semi-supervised object detection
- The open-set problem in unlabeled data
- Prior work on open-set SSL and the first OSSOD method
- Remaining challenges of that method
- Our proposed method
- Results and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- SSL helps image recognition by using lots of unlabeled data (several refs)
  - object detection also benefits -> various SSOD methods
- Open-set problem
  - SSOD assumes unlabeled and labeled data share label space
  - unrealistic: real unlabeled data has OOD samples (Fig. 1 (a))
  - detectors classify OOD as ID -> performance drops
- Prior work
  - open-set methods for image classification exist, hard to transfer: image-level vs instance-level task
  - one paper first tackles open set in detection, names it OSSOD
  - existing OOD detection methods applied directly -> unsatisfactory
  - first OSSOD method: separate OOD detection network trained on labeled data, filters OOD instances during pseudo-labeling
- Remaining challenges
  - only labeled data for OOD network; real OODs only in unlabeled data -> suboptimal (Fig. 1 (b-1))
  - manual threshold, time-consuming per dataset
  - separate training, extra backbone -> inefficient
- Our method
  - semi-supervised outlier filtering: labeled + unlabeled data
  - error accumulation problem: mispredicted pseudo-labels accumulate; OOD mispredicted as ID (blue cats) -> boundary expands (Fig. 1 (b-2))
  - Dual Competing OOD (DCO) head: two competing sub-heads (Fig. 1 (b-3)); no manual threshold
  - whole framework online end-to-end trainable
- Results / contributions
  - SOTA OSSOD on several benchmarks; easily applied to other SSOD frameworks
  - bullet list: outlier filtering; DCO head vs error accumulation; online end-to-end framework

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Semi-supervised learning (SSL) improves the performance of various image recognition tasks a lot by using a large amount of unlabeled data that is available. Object detection has also benefited a lot from SSL, and various semi-supervised object detection (SSOD) methods have been proposed.

But current SSOD methods make a strong assumption that the unlabeled data and the labeled data are from the same label space. This assumption is not very realistic in practice, because unlabeled datasets in the real world usually have the open-set problem, which means there are OOD samples, as shown in Fig. 1 (a). The object detectors in current SSOD methods will wrongly classify OOD samples as ID classes and in the end the performance gets worse.

Some works have been proposed to deal with this problem in image classification. But these methods are hard to apply directly to object detection, because image classification is an image-level task while object detection is an instance-level task, which is more challenging. One previous paper is the first to tackle the open-set problem in object detection, and they name it the OSSOD task. They tried applying existing OOD detection methods directly but found the performance was not satisfactory. Then they proposed the first OSSOD method, which trains a separate OOD detection network with labeled data to distinguish and filter out OOD instances for the SSOD framework during pseudo-labeling.

They have improved the performance on open-set unlabeled data, but there are still some challenges to address. First, they only use labeled data to train the OOD detection network. But in the OSSOD task, the real OOD instances are only in the unlabeled data. Because real OODs are missing, the performance is suboptimal, as shown in Fig. 1 (b-1). Second, they need a manual threshold for the OOD detection network to filter out OOD instances. Searching for the best threshold for each dataset takes a lot of time. Third, their OOD detection network has to be trained separately from the object detector and needs an additional backbone, which is inefficient for the training process and for the network complexity.

Our method:
- semi-supervised outlier filtering strategy, uses labeled + unlabeled data
- error accumulation problem: mispredictions in pseudo-labels accumulate; OOD mispredicted as ID (the blue cats) -> decision boundary expands, Fig. 1 (b-2)
- Dual Competing OOD (DCO) head: two sub-heads in competition, Fig. 1 (b-3); no manual threshold
- whole OSSOD framework online end-to-end trainable

Results and contributions:
- SOTA OSSOD performance on several benchmarks; easy to apply to other SSOD frameworks
- contribution bullets: outlier filtering strategy; DCO head against error accumulation; online end-to-end framework, SOTA, applicable to other SSOD frameworks

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Semi-supervised learning (SSL) improves the performance of various image recognition tasks a lot by using a large amount of unlabeled data that is available. Object detection has also benefited a lot from SSL, and various semi-supervised object detection (SSOD) methods have been proposed.

But current SSOD methods make a strong assumption that the unlabeled data and the labeled data are from the same label space. This assumption is not very realistic in practice, because unlabeled datasets in the real world usually have the open-set problem, which means there are OOD samples, as shown in Fig. 1 (a). The object detectors in current SSOD methods will wrongly classify OOD samples as ID classes and in the end the performance gets worse.

Some works have been proposed to deal with this problem in image classification. But these methods are hard to apply directly to object detection, because image classification is an image-level task while object detection is an instance-level task, which is more challenging. One previous paper is the first to tackle the open-set problem in object detection, and they name it the OSSOD task. They tried applying existing OOD detection methods directly but found the performance was not satisfactory. Then they proposed the first OSSOD method, which trains a separate OOD detection network with labeled data to distinguish and filter out OOD instances for the SSOD framework during pseudo-labeling.

They have improved the performance on open-set unlabeled data, but there are still some challenges to address. First, they only use labeled data to train the OOD detection network. But in the OSSOD task, the real OOD instances are only in the unlabeled data. Because real OODs are missing, the performance is suboptimal, as shown in Fig. 1 (b-1). Second, they need a manual threshold for the OOD detection network to filter out OOD instances. Searching for the best threshold for each dataset takes a lot of time. Third, their OOD detection network has to be trained separately from the object detector and needs an additional backbone, which is inefficient for the training process and for the network complexity.

To address these issues, we propose a new OSSOD method. 1) We propose a semi-supervised outlier filtering strategy that uses both labeled and unlabeled data to improve the OOD filtering ability. 2) We also identify the error accumulation problem, where the mispredictions in pseudo-labels accumulate during semi-supervised outlier filtering. As shown in Fig. 1 (b-2), when OOD instances are mispredicted as ID (the blue cats), the decision boundary expands and more OOD labels get misclassified. To deal with this, we propose the Dual Competing OOD (DCO) head, which has two sub-heads that form a competitive relationship during semi-supervised learning, as shown in Fig. 1 (b-3). This mitigates the issue and improves the performance further. Also, the DCO head does not need any manual threshold for filtering OOD instances. 3) We make the whole OSSOD framework online end-to-end trainable.

The experimental results on several benchmarks show that our method can achieve state-of-the-art OSSOD performance. Also, our method can easily be applied to other SSOD frameworks to boost their performance. In summary, the contributions of this paper are:

- • We propose a semi-supervised outlier filtering strategy, which improves OSSOD accuracy by making better use of the unlabeled data.

- • We identify the error accumulation problem in semi-supervised outlier filtering and mitigate it with the Dual Competing OOD head, which does not need a threshold.

- • These two components make up an online end-to-end OSSOD framework. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on several OSSOD benchmarks and can be applied to other SSOD frameworks.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Semi-supervised learning (SSL) significantly improves the performance of various image recognition tasks by utilizing a large amount of available unlabeled data [1,2,3,4,5]. Object detection performance has also benefited greatly from SSL, and various semi-supervised object detection (SSOD) methods have been proposed [6,7,8,9,10,11].

However, current SSOD methods rely on a strong assumption that the unlabeled and labeled data come from the same label space. This assumption is somewhat unrealistic in practice, because unlabeled datasets in the real world usually face the open-set problem, i.e. they contain OOD samples, as shown in Fig. 1 (a). Object detectors in current SSOD methods will mistakenly classify OOD samples as ID classes, which ultimately degrades the performance.

Some works [5,12] have been proposed to tackle this problem in the image classification task. However, these methods are difficult to apply directly to object detection, since image classification is an image-level task while object detection is a more challenging instance-level task. The paper of [13] is the first to tackle the open-set problem in object detection and names it the OSSOD task. They tried to apply existing OOD detection methods directly but found the performance unsatisfactory. They then proposed the first OSSOD method, training a separate OOD detection network with labeled data to distinguish and filter out OOD instances for the SSOD framework during pseudo-labeling.

Although they improved the performance on open-set unlabeled data, some challenges still need to be addressed. First, they only use labeled data to train the OOD detection network, while in the OSSOD task real OOD instances only exist in unlabeled data. The lack of real OODs results in suboptimal performance, as shown in Fig. 1 (b-1). Second, they need a manual threshold for the OOD detection network to filter out OOD instances, and searching for the best threshold for each dataset is time-consuming. Third, their OOD detection network must be trained separately from the object detector and requires an additional backbone, which is inefficient in terms of the training process and network complexity.

To address these issues, we propose a novel OSSOD method: 1) We propose a semi-supervised outlier filtering strategy that improves OOD filtering ability by leveraging both labeled and unlabeled data. 2) We further identify the error accumulation problem: the mispredictions in pseudo-labels accumulate during semi-supervised outlier filtering. As shown in Fig. 1 (b-2), once OOD instances are mispredicted as ID (the blue cats), the decision boundary expands and misclassifies more OOD labels. To tackle this, we propose the Dual Competing OOD (DCO) head, which mitigates this issue with two sub-heads that form a competitive relationship during semi-supervised learning, as shown in Fig. 1 (b-3), and further improves the performance. Meanwhile, the DCO head requires no manual threshold for filtering OOD instances. 3) We make the entire OSSOD framework online end-to-end trainable.

Experimental results on several benchmarks show that our method achieves state-of-the-art OSSOD performance. Moreover, our method can be easily applied to other SSOD frameworks to boost their performance. In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:

- • We propose a semi-supervised outlier filtering strategy, which improves OSSOD accuracy by better utilizing the unlabeled data.

- • We further identify the error accumulation problem in semi-supervised outlier filtering and mitigate it with the threshold-free Dual Competing OOD head.

- • Together, these two components form an online end-to-end OSSOD framework. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on several OSSOD benchmarks and can be applied to other SSOD frameworks.
